The assessment considers sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities that have the potential to influence CBA’s ability to create value over the short to medium term (1–5 years). This year’s assessment reviewed a range of sustainability topics, which were prioritised using our 5x5 risk matrix and exercised significant judgement. The prioritised topics were then grouped into overarching themes that informed the structure of this report. Theme selection involved significant judgement, guided by the results of our materiality assessment. Meaningfully delivering on our purpose As Australia’s leading retail and business bank, we play an important role in supporting our customers and helping the nation prosper. We are committed to improving living standards for all Australians. By remaining a strong, safe and resilient bank, we can continue lending to our customers through economic cycles, investing for the future, and delivering sustainable returns for our shareholders. Rising geopolitical tensions, global economic challenges, and technological changes are causing many of our customers to feel financial pressure and uncertainty about their futures. Community concerns about housing and energy affordability, as well as intergenerational inequality, continue to grow. Australia’s economy remains resilient and relatively well positioned. Our country is still an attractive place to live, work and invest. We face headwinds which highlight the need for long-term economic reform and call for a confident vision for growth, fiscal responsibility with future generations in mind, and supply-side reform in areas like housing and energy. Australia also needs to maintain sovereignty of nationally important industries, including Australia’s financial system. Governments and industries need to work together to address challenging domestic issues and deliver a stronger future for Australia. Learn more about our operating context on pages 10–11. Refreshing our strategy We have made progress in our strategy to support customers through changing economic conditions. This year we lent $42 billion to businesses to help them grow and assisted over 140,000 households in buying a home. We have strengthened our focus on customer experience and consistently invested in leading technology and data capabilities. Importantly, we have continued to become a safer organisation with greater risk maturity, transparency and discipline. However, we know there is much more to do. Our operating context has shifted, and we expect the next decade to bring complex geopolitical, reputational and competitive challenges. To better navigate the future, we have refreshed our strategy to continue positioning the Bank to deliver for our customers, communities, the nation and our shareholders. Our strategy considers diverse sustainability-related impacts, helping us address environmental, social, and governance risks and opportunities. We are making decisions today with a focus on long-term outcomes, even when they come at a short-term cost. We want to help build Australia’s future economy by supporting business growth and productivity. Productivity is key to improving living standards and its benefits need to be shared fairly so all communities can prosper. We are committed to allocating capital intentionally, ensuring banking services remain accessible, and advocating for a strong financial system and an economy that works for all Australians. Many Australians and Australian businesses trust us with their transaction banking and deposit relationship. We want to deliver experiences our customers value and continually deepen our relationships with

Delivering for our customers Being the trusted financial partner for Australian retail and business customers remains key to our strategy and long-term success. We continue to support customers with a range of money management tools and educational materials. For customers facing financial difficulty, we have initiated more than 139,000 tailored payment arrangements. To serve a broad range of customers we are focused on delivering a better, safer and more efficient banking experience. Our purpose, building a brighter future for all, reflects our enduring commitment to Australia. It inspires us to be better for our customers, people and communities, and shows our optimism for the future. By maintaining our balance sheet strength and executing our strategy we can deliver on our purpose. 6 MESSAGE FROM OUR CHAIR AND CEO We offer the largest branch and ATM network, Australia-based call centres and the nation’s most popular banking app. This year we extended our commitment to regional Australia, keeping all regional branches open until at least mid-2027, and converted 15 Western Australian Bankwest branches to be CBA-branded. During the year we have constructively participated in national policy discussions and advocated for changes that support safe, secure and reliable banking services. To keep pace with technological change, we invested $2.3 billion in modernising our systems, migrating data, and building world-class engineering and AI capabilities. With persistently high levels of fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime, we have invested over $900 million this year to help protect our customers. We have also reduced customer fraud and scam losses by 76% since peak losses in late 2022. We continue to work with other organisations and Government to build national resilience against these threats which continue to impact too many customers. Supporting a prosperous, resilient and optimistic nation A strong and resilient financial system is required to support a strong economy. Financial services play a vital role in our customers’ everyday lives. Disruptions and outages in banking services prevent customers from making payments or running their businesses. We also play an important role to support economic growth by lending to businesses. Maintaining strong capital and prudent balance sheet settings enables us to maintain necessary investment to deliver resilient and safe banking services, and support our customers and the economy. We carefully consider funding, credit and liquidity needs and monitor non-financial risks such as operational resilience, compliance with laws and regulations, and broader environmental and social risks. Australia needs a financial system that works for all stakeholders and inspires optimism about the future. We continue to share customer insights and other perspectives to help inform policies that can support a strong financial system and economy. Delivering sustainable performance Our financial results reflect our customer focus and disciplined execution of our strategic priorities. Our strong financial position enables us to continue supporting our customers and deliver a sustainable dividend. We have declared a final dividend of $2.60 per share, fully franked. Learn more about our financial performance on pages 26–33. Outlook We know many of our customers are still cautious with global volatility creating uncertainty. The Australian economy has remained resilient with strong fundamentals. Looking ahead, there are many reasons to feel optimistic about Australia’s future including modest economic growth, a healthy labour market and easing interest rates. Our role is to support our customers and the nation. We will stay focused on investing in our business and executing our strategy to bring our purpose to life. We will continue to work with key stakeholders to advocate for issues that are in the national interest, and policy settings that help sustainably support services that Australians value. Macroeconomic and cost-of-living pressures Australia’s economy has continued to show resilience, supported by strong population growth along with healthy labour market conditions. While overall conditions remain strong, some household budgets, particularly for younger Australians, renters and mortgage holders, continue to face pressures from elevated interest rates, rising essential costs and housing affordability challenges. During the year inflation continued to ease within the Reserve Bank of Australia’s (RBA) target range allowing the RBA to start reducing official interest rates. While economic growth continues, rising public sector expenditure and low levels of productivity growth highlight the growing need for long-term economic reform. We maintain a conservative balance sheet, with capital, funding, and credit settings carefully managed to ensure resilience and ongoing support for our customers and the broader economy. Heightened geopolitical risks The global geopolitical environment continues to change with heightened tensions and policy uncertainty weighing on trade, energy and investment markets. Increasing global trade restrictions, strategic competition and regional conflicts are disrupting supply chains, limiting access to key technologies and reshaping capital flows. Cyber threats and attacks continue to evolve, requiring heightened vigilance by people and businesses. Australia’s banking system remains resilient. We actively assess downside scenarios through robust stress testing, scenario analysis, and balance sheet risk management to strengthen operational resilience and safeguard against potential shocks. The Bank is well positioned to navigate external challenges and continue supporting our customers and the broader economy. 10 Evolving technology Advances in AI, data analytics and digital infrastructure are transforming the banking landscape. These technologies offer opportunities to enhance customer experience, streamline processes, and improve risk management and operational efficiency. At the same time, they introduce new risks – including cyber security threats, scams, privacy concerns and the use of AI. Rapidly adopting technology such as AI to modernise existing industries and build new industries is critical for our economy. Careful consideration will be needed to incentivise productive investment, build sovereign capability and retain economic benefits in Australia for all Australians. Customers are increasingly seeking personalised, high-value experiences and seamless service. Pricing pressure remains evident across deposits and lending, where customer demand for value and changing channel dynamics contribute to a highly competitive environment. We continue to see large technology firms expand their presence, especially in payments and small business segments. As more customers engage through digital channels, delivering efficient, high-quality service at scale to all Australians is essential. Continued investment in technology and innovation helps us to meet these expectations while maintaining our operational resilience. Maintaining our position as Australia’s leading bank requires a consistent focus on our customers – building trusted relationships and continuing to invest in technology, data, and insights to deliver personalised and value-added experiences. Trust and reputation Trust is fundamental to long-term value creation and building strong customer relationships. Many Australians and Australian businesses trust us with their transaction banking and deposit relationship. This requires a continued focus on being safe and strong. As a bank, we are inherently exposed to reputational risk with issues such as data privacy, conduct and governance having the potential to quickly erode stakeholder confidence. Expectations continue to rise around transparency, the responsible use of data and AI, and the delivery of fairer and responsible outcomes. Stakeholders are also increasingly focused on how we support Australia’s economy and contribute to financial inclusion and broader community outcomes. The Bank has an important role to play. We are working closely with government and industry to support more sustainable outcomes for our customers and communities. These efforts are fundamental to maintaining financial system stability and resilience, and to supporting the long-term health of the Australian economy and society. Helping build Australia’s future economy Helping the nation prosper and improving living standards for all Australians. Supporting our customers and communities The past few years have been challenging for Australian households and businesses, with higher inflation and cost-of-living pressures. We remain committed to supporting our customers, communities and the nation when they need us most. We maintained our focus on supporting customers with a range of options, which included improved access to hardship assistance and over 139,000 tailored payment arrangements for those most in need. More than three million customers each month use our digital money management tools to help them manage their finances. Keeping customers’ accounts safe and secure remains a priority. We invested more than $900 million this year to help protect our customers from fraud, scams, cyber threats and financial crime. Our continued investment helped reduce customer fraud and scam losses by over 30% this year. We acknowledge there is still more to be done. Message from our Chair Board strategic priorities This year the Board has again spent considerable time challenging our strategy settings given our operating context and the strategic risks that affect our operations. We have met with a broad range of stakeholders to provide perspective and challenge our thinking on risks and opportunities. These have included customers, employees, policy makers and energy companies. Our refreshed strategy elevates our focus on supporting the national agenda, prioritises investment in technology that provides customers with better, faster and safer banking, and invests in our people and branches to better serve our customers and communities. With challenging domestic issues and heightened geopolitical tensions, it is more important than ever that our financial institutions have strong and resilient balance sheets and take a long-term approach to decision making. Learn more about our strategy on pages 16–25. Financial system resilience, balance sheet strength and organic capital generation Global events and previous cycles have taught us the value of having funding flexibility, strong provisions, appropriate capital levels and balance sheet strength. Shocks are difficult to foresee but can drive up funding costs and result in a loss of confidence in financial institutions. Economic downturns put pressure on asset quality, profitability and capital. The resilience of the economy is linked to the resilience of our financial system. A strong banking system is dependent on banks maintaining strong balance sheets. The Board fully supports management decisions that strengthen our balance sheet rather than temporarily maximise short-term earnings. History has also taught us that sustained profitability which generates organic capital underpins strong investor support for the sector. This enables banks to fund the country and ensure an equitable approach to rates for our depositors and mortgage holders. Being the ‘Bank for all Australians’ is at the heart of our strategy. However, there is a real cost to providing financial services including branches and ATMs, our people, call centres, cash transit and regulatory compliance. To sustainably deliver good outcomes for our customers, people and communities, we also need to generate shareholder returns. Our purpose and refreshed strategy focuses us on supporting Australia’s prosperity over the coming decade. With continuing global uncertainty, our long-term decision making and strong balance sheet positions CBA to support our customers and the nation. role in appointing the CEO and ensuring appropriate succession plans. Attracting, developing and retaining Executive talent with the right skills and values, at all levels, is needed to deliver our strategic ambition and enhance franchise value. The Board engages with the Executive Leadership Team (ELT) regularly. The People & Remuneration Committee reviews Executives’ performance through robust discussions to determine remuneration outcomes. It is not uncommon to hear from shareholders that they would like to see a performance and remuneration framework with greater weighting given to financial measures, to incentivise stronger alignment to shareholder returns. We agree with APRA that non-financial measures are important. We recognise the risk that a framework with more emphasis on earnings may bias management to make short-term decisions that are not in the long-term interests of shareholders, customers and the wider Australian economy. The Board has designed our framework to provide the right balance between delivering shareholder returns, customer outcomes and investing for the future. Our frameworks enable us to hold management to account and not overweight any one factor. Our long-term remuneration is designed to support a collective focus on generating sustainable long-term value and comply with requirements under APRA Prudential Standard CPS 511. Through the granting of equity instruments with long vesting periods, we reinforce the alignment of Executives’ experience with that of our shareholders. For example, when shareholder returns are less favourable, Executives share the impact in lower vesting outcomes and a reduction in the value of their long-term holdings, although we acknowledge the outcome for Executives can still be positive. Learn more about our approach to remuneration on pages 182–218. Our skills matrix is regularly reviewed. Risk management in action The Board-approved risk appetite statement (RAS) establishes the level of risk we must operate in to deliver our strategy. Our Risk Management Framework (RMF) outlines the Bank’s expectations on how we identify, measure, monitor and respond to our risks. Our RMF is comprised of systems, structures, policies, processes and people. They work together to help identify, assess and mitigate our internal and external sources of risk. We categorise the material risks the Bank is exposed to as strategic, financial and non-financial risks. Each material risk type has its own specific framework or requirements to manage the risk. These material risks and our approach to managing them are set out in our RMF. The RMF is reviewed annually by the ELT and the Board. The RMF is also independently reviewed every three years by an external reviewer, supported by internal and external audit programs. These reviews of the RMF as well as our annual RMD to APRA, set out our plans to strengthen the RMF in support of our strategy. The RMF enablers facilitate the effective identification, measurement, monitoring and response to our material risks. They help us translate the RAS into our daily business activities. Risk governance and reporting The Board has ultimate responsibility for the Bank’s risk governance, including the RMF and its implementation by management. The Board is supported by its four Committees as well as management-level committees that oversee our material risks. Management regularly provides information to the Board which allows material risk positions to be monitored against the RAS and policy limits. Risk accountabilities and skills The Three Lines of Accountability model (3LoA) organises our accountabilities to manage the Bank’s risks by separating the roles. Line 1 own and manage the risks whereas Line 2 develop risk frameworks and provide assurance. Line 3 provide independent assurance over how effectively risks are being managed. The 3LoA include skilled employees within each line and are supported by risk capabilities, and performance and remuneration frameworks. Our remuneration framework supports accountability by incorporating risk assessment as gate openers and modifiers in employee and executive remuneration. Risk infrastructure and data Our risk infrastructure provides the systems, tools, models and data required for the effective management of our material risks. Risk culture Our risk culture reflects our beliefs and behaviours within the Bank and determines how we identify, measure, monitor and respond to risks. These behaviours guide decision making and good risk management, and embody our values and leadership principles. This helps our actions align to our core beliefs. To sustain and improve our risk culture, senior management and the Board form a view of the Bank’s risk culture through an annual Board risk culture assessment. This is supported by the Group risk culture response plan, which addresses areas of focus identified by the Board. It is further reinforced by self-reflections on business unit risk culture to drive improvement at the team level. Risk measurement We use multiple techniques to identify and measure risks the Bank is exposed to. These include stress testing and scenario analysis; risk and control self-assessments; compliance self-assessments; emerging risk assessment; systems and models to quantify risks and identify risk exceptions; assurance of the RMF in the form of Line 1 controls testing; Line 2 assurance reviews and framework approvals; Line 3 internal audits; and the external audit program. Stress testing Stress testing and scenario analysis are important risk management tools. They enable the Board and senior management to better understand, quantify and manage risks. They also inform how we may respond to risk events occurring and any potential weaknesses in our actions during a crisis. The results of these stress tests are important for strengthening our risk management approach. Stress testing results also inform our risk appetite and assist us in identifying the acceptable levels of risk we will assume in our operations. Our emerging risks While remaining vigilant to the risks we need to manage today, we also look ahead to identify potential future challenges. We aim to uphold the risk management standards expected by our customers, communities, regulators and shareholders, both now and in the future. Emerging risks are risks that are either newly developing or already exist, but their effects have not yet been substantially realised. These risks are often constantly evolving and have the potential to impact the Bank and our customers in the medium to long term (over 12 months). It is essential to respond to these risks now to minimise their potential future impact. Emerging risks are often driven by new trends in our operating environment, such as competition, new technologies, regulation or evolving customer expectations. Our emerging risk profile is updated annually through a review process with the ELT and the Board. This process aligns with the annual review of the Bank’s strategy. The emerging risk process evaluates the adequacy of the Bank’s mitigation strategies to prevent emerging risks from materially impacting the Bank. In cases where we may have limited ability to influence emerging risks, it may be more challenging to implement effective mitigative actions. This may require us to take additional steps to address these risks. The emerging risk themes the Board and ELT focused on this year are outlined below. Geopolitical conflict and macroeconomic uncertainty Our operations face risks from global political events, such as elections and policy changes, civil unrest, international competition and conflicts. These disruptions can increase social pressures domestically; affect unemployment, housing supply, and market volatility; and escalate credit and operational risks for financial institutions. Failure to prepare for these geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainties could heighten our exposure to various financial and non-financial risks, which we monitor and manage through our RMF. Emerging technology Innovation driven by emerging and disruptive technology, including AI, continues to rapidly evolve. As we pursue our strategy, which includes a focus on technology and AI, we continue working hard to effectively manage risks from change implementation that could lead to service disruptions, poor customer experiences, fraud and scams, conduct issues, cyber security threats, and data and privacy issues. As a Bank, we invest in governance and risk initiatives to support our AI goals, including for responsible AI. Cyber security threats The Bank anticipates cyber attacks to persist and grow as adversaries use new technologies such as GenAI to exploit vulnerabilities, including third parties and cloud environments. These could lead to compromised customer data, critical systems disruptions and potential breaches of our obligations. We continue to strengthen our cyber security risk management through dedicated teams that monitor and respond to potential cyber security threats, applying learnings

and risk initiatives to support our AI goals, including for responsible AI. Regulatory reforms Upcoming regulatory reforms could significantly impact us and our customers, spanning areas like Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Terrorism Financing (AML/CTF), cyber security, scams, privacy, payments licensing, AI and climate disclosures. To prepare for new regulation, we frequently evaluate our obligations including those under the new Scam Prevention Framework Act 2025 (Cth), which will be further supported by industry specific codes, not yet released. The Bank is also improving its security infrastructure for fraud and scams, and forming partnerships to better handle scam phishing and reporting within the industry ecosystem. Energy transition in Australia Australia’s economy needs affordable and reliable energy. Replacing coal-fired power with firmed renewable energy is crucial to meet Australia’s renewable energy targets. With 90% of coal-fired power stations expected to retire by 2035, delays in replacement generation could increase electricity price volatility, affect reliability and have broader economic impacts. Credit risks could also be heightened for the Bank, as well as disruptions to our operations. We continue to engage with Government on the energy transition and support retail and business customers finance existing technologies, such as rooftop solar, batteries and electric vehicles to help reduce their emissions. This also helps reduce reliance on large-scale utility investments. Growing societal pressures impacting our customers and communities The Bank continues to face heightened expectations from governments, regulators and the community to respond to key challenges including cost-of-living pressures, housing affordability and crisis support. Many Australians are feeling the impact of rising fraud and scams activity, as well as ongoing affordability concerns. Our annual materiality assessment seeks to identify sustainability topics that are most relevant to our stakeholders and CBA. Insights from the assessment are shared across the Bank and with the Board, to help inform decision making and our sustainability disclosures. The assessment considers CBA’s operating environment and uses insights from our stakeholder engagement. Internal subject matter experts, representing key stakeholder groups, assess proposed topics based on their direct engagement with stakeholders. Each topic is evaluated for its relevance to Australia’s economy, environment and people, and CBA’s impact on or ability to influence the topic (impact materiality), as well as the topic’s potential impact on CBA’s financial performance (financial materiality). This year the Bank reached out to customers through NetBank, the CommBank app, news articles, social media, in-branch community sessions and campaigns. Research commissioned by CBA revealed that while 90% of Australians believe that talking about scams with loved ones can raise awareness, only 8% felt comfortable having a discussion with family about being scammed. To help bridge this gap, CBA launched a new education campaign that aims to encourage conversations about the dangers of scams between generations. By addressing intergenerational knowledge gaps, it seeks to empower all Australians, particularly older generations, with the information and tools needed to help them stay safe. How can I help? Have regular conversations about scams with family and friends. Stay informed about the latest scam tactics. Remember to implement and educate others on three simple steps to help prevent scams: 1. Stop: Does a call, email or text seem off? The best thing to do is stop and take a breath. Real organisations will not put you under pressure to act instantly. 2. Check: Ask someone you trust or contact the organisation the message claims to be from. 3. Reject: If unsure, hang up on the caller, delete the email, block the phone number. Change your password if you think someone else may have it, and make sure you pick something long and unique. Contact your bank immediately if you suspect a scam. Improving payments regulation Delivering a safe, reliable and efficient payments system is a regulatory priority. We welcomed the RBA review of merchant card payment costs and surcharging as an opportunity to deliver better outcomes for consumers and small businesses. Customer preferences towards contactless payments and ecommerce is growing with electronic payments being the lowest cost form of payment to accept for merchants. It is important that payment regulation applies to popular payment solutions such as digital wallets and buy-now-pay-later services. To simplify the system, we support removing surcharging for both credit and debit cards with safeguards so that small businesses are supported and benefit from lower costs. With interchange fees supporting a range of benefits valued by customers and merchants, appropriate pricing and economics across the payments ecosystem is essential for a safe, reliable, sustainable and innovative payments system. The interaction between these policy changes and proposed legislative changes to the Payment Systems (Regulation) Act 1998 are important and complex. The RBA is consulting to ensure there are no unintended consequences and any changes are in the best interest of Australia’s payments ecosystem and end users. Keeping our customers safe Keeping our customers safe is a priority. This year we commenced rollout of multi-factor authentication (MFA) as an added layer of protection against unauthorised access to customers’ accounts and to keep their money safe. We began our phased rollout of MFA in April 2025 to our NetBank registered customers who are also CommBank app registered. Once enrolled, each time a customer logs into online banking, they will need to confirm the login attempt through our CommBank app. Vigilance on cyber security Cyber resilience and information security remain key priorities for the Bank. As cyber threats become more frequent and complex, we continue to invest in strategies, advanced technologies such as AI and GenAI, and skilled teams to help protect our customers, assets and data. This year we enhanced the resilience of our cloud infrastructure and improved key cyber control operations. For example, we implemented near real-time code scanning to help detect and mitigate risks associated with sensitive information in our code. We are adopting AI tools to help detect and neutralise external threats more efficiently. We also worked with our suppliers to enhance their data and system security, helping to further strengthen our own resilience. To help support system-wide resilience and strengthen the national security ecosystem, we engage closely with Government and industry. Alongside industry partners, we contributed to a consultation process that led to the introduction of Australia’s first standalone cyber security law – the Cyber Security Act 2024. We also collaborated with the Tech Council of Australia and the Group of Eight Australian Universities on the inaugural Australian Cyber Exchange 2025, which aimed to showcase and strengthen Australia’s sovereign cyber security capabilities. We continue to strengthen our cyber resilience by regularly reviewing and testing our approach, as well as engaging external firms to assess and provide feedback. We look to integrate insights from these assessments into our risk mitigation strategies to help enhance our protective and defensive capabilities. We consider cyber security a shared responsibility across the Bank. Our people play a key role by helping build secure processes and products, and effectively identifying and responding to cyber threats. Investing in technology and innovation to deliver seamless, secure and personalised digital experiences. Digitisation, innovation and artificial intelligence Accelerating innovation with AI Factory We recently launched the AI Factory, our platform for safely testing, developing, and scaling advanced AI models on our proprietary data. Built on Amazon Web Services (AWS) latest infrastructure, it enables our teams to train and fine-tune AI models faster and more efficiently. The AI Factory helps support increased scale, performance and sophistication in GenAI use cases by addressing Australian language and banking nuances. We can now process data at an unprecedented scale enabling us to run a deep learning model over 3 trillion data points across 4 billion transactions. Generating one million data points is 50% faster and requires 90% less compute time because of our transition from Central Processing Units (CPUs) to Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). GPU-based models can transcribe approximately 100,000 call centre interactions in 15 hours, a task that would have previously taken three times as long. Message from our Chair and CEO Meeting Australia’s 2030 interim emissions reduction target requires significant investment. Estimates suggest Australia’s transition to net zero needs more than $600 billion of investment by 2050 to decarbonise the nation’s industry and energy systems. CBA can support our customers to fund their transition. The energy sector continues to be the biggest contributor to Australia’s domestic emissions. We believe that affordably decarbonising Australia’s electricity grid remains the most important step for Australia. Australia’s future economy needs more affordable and reliable energy Historically, Australia has been a reliable energy producer and exporter, making affordable energy prices a competitive advantage. As we transition to a net zero economy, we need to maintain this advantage to support Australian living standards and help build a brighter future for all. The demand for electricity in Australia is increasing due to economic and population growth, increased digitisation and electrification. Access to affordable and reliable energy sources is needed to support Australia’s prosperity and future economy. While progress on meeting Australia’s renewable energy target is commendable, over reliance on one energy source can lead to vulnerabilities in our electricity markets, blackouts and increased costs, putting more pressure on energy bills. We welcome the Australian Energy Market Operator’s (AEMO) work on approaches to grid stability. All energy sources and grid stability approaches have trade-offs such as emissions intensity, cost, time-to build and impacts on nature. We see an important role for governments and industries to balance and communicate those trade-offs and develop sound policies. Building community support for Australia’s transition to net zero is important. We welcome policies that can help Australia deliver more affordable and reliable energy for all Australians, now and into the future. Balancing trade-offs to support the transition Australia needs effective climate change policies that reduce emissions, provide investment certainty, support economic growth, and minimise increased costs for essential goods such as food and electricity. Energy security is crucial to the success of the Australian economy. Australia is facing a critical moment in the energy transition, needing to deliver important national energy infrastructure that lowers emissions quickly and affordably. Limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels appears increasingly difficult and the pathway to net zero, globally, is looking narrower. The Australian Government is continuing to develop a national Net Zero Plan to guide our country’s transition to meet our legislated target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Australia’s transition to a net zero economy by 2050 is underway. Government policies, and new generation and transmission infrastructure are assisting. As the bank for all Australians, we remain committed to helping our customers and supporting Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050. 102 CLIMATE DISCLOSURES Progress on our

We set our first operational emissions targets in 2009 and our first sector-level financed emissions targets in 2022. We take meeting our commitments seriously. We are pleased to have achieved our 2025 Scope 1 and 2, and Scope 3 operational emissions reduction targets, and to be on track for 12 of our sector-level financed emissions goals and targets. Since commencing our journey we have continued to learn more about sector-level pathways, actions we can take and key dependencies in achieving our targets. Stakeholders have noted that some of our sector-level financed emissions targets are dependent on external factors, including decarbonisation of Australia’s electricity grid. As we prepare for new sustainability reporting, including required disclosures on climate targets, we have taken the opportunity to clarify our aspirations as targets or goals. We considered factors like CBA’s control or influence, as well as key external dependencies, challenges or assumptions. As a result, some previously reported targets are now described as goals. We believe this change gives stakeholders greater clarity on how we will achieve our goals and targets, and helps to enhance the accuracy and transparency of our reporting. Our goals and targets remain aligned to 1.5°C scenarios. We believe this continues to be the right setting against which to track our progress. We remain committed to achieving our goals and targets and continue to monitor progress. Although we reassessed the feasibility of sector-level financed emissions targets for the Australian agriculture sector, we have not set any new goals or targets this year. For a summary of our goals and targets, see pages 162–163. Supporting Australia’s energy transition As Australia’s economy and population grows, households and businesses electrify, and digitisation increases, the demand for electricity will continue to grow. A reliable and affordable electricity grid is integral to the economy and Australia’s future prosperity. Electricity accounts for around 34% of Australia’s emissions. Decarbonising the electricity grid is critical to the decarbonisation of other sectors, including housing – the largest sector that CBA finances. For Australia, and the Bank, to achieve its emissions reduction ambitions, the electricity grid needs to decarbonise. Replacing coal-fired power stations with renewables is challenging. The nation needs to address long planning timeframes, supply chain constraints and increase community support for infrastructure. Installing rooftop solar remains popular with consumers. The Government’s renewable energy target provided Australia with direction. Recent policies including the Capacity Investment Scheme and Rewiring the Nation are helping to accelerate the transition. With generation capacity and transmission infrastructure progressing, Australia is better placed to meet its 2030 target of a 43% reduction in emissions below 2005 levels. It is our understanding that Australia should be able to produce sufficient generation to meet growing demand over the next decade, provided current State and Federal Government projects to build renewable and dispatchable generation, transmission assets and policies to coordinate consumer energy resources eventuate. Ongoing monitoring, policy adjustments and managing new challenges are essential for helping Australia remain on track. Achieving Australia’s emissions targets and producing reliable, affordable energy requires effective community engagement and policies that seek to maintain our country’s energy advantage. Affordably decarbonising Australia’s electricity grid is essential for Australia’s economy. 104 CLIMATE DISCLOSURES Reducing emissions in key sectors Australia’s Climate Change Authority (CCA) has published six sector pathways. 1 The CCA’s report identifies potential technologies and actions for each sector that, taken together, could deliver net zero emissions for Australia by 2050. The CCA recognises that emissions must fall across all sectors, however each sector is on a different pathway to net zero by 2050. For some sectors, like power generation, with coordinated planning, the pathway may be steep and rapid as technologies are mature and ready to scale. Sectors like agriculture, however, are expected to experience a slower and more gradual path as technologies are in early development. Government policy support and investment are needed to accelerate the deployment of early-stage technologies and actions. Maintaining system reliability and stability Renewable energy generation is increasing. However, high electricity costs remain a concern for consumers and businesses. Australia needs to find affordable ways to achieve its 2030 renewable energy target and maintain system stability. We continue to support AEMO’s view that flexible gas-powered generation is crucial in a high renewable electricity system. Along with batteries and pumped hydro, gas can provide critical backup to variable renewable energy, reliability as coal-fired power stations retire, and flexibility to adapt to demand changes. Gas plants, capable of rapid startup, help to provide continuous electricity supply and support grid reliability and stability, especially during high-demand periods and extreme weather. Australians broadly support a focus on the nation’s climate change ambitions but are concerned about the impact on their cost of living and quality of life. The transition requires government and industry to balance and communicate competing trade-offs between energy sources. Our role in helping to build Australia’s future economy Climate change can have a significant impact on the Australian economy and our communities. Given one in three Australians and one in four Australian businesses call us their main financial institution, our role is to help build Australia’s future economy by supporting our customers and communities as they navigate the choices they need to make to transition to a lower-carbon economy. While climate change is not currently estimated to be financially material to the Bank in the short term, it is important that our climate strategy aligns to our purpose. This means supporting our customers as they take action to adapt to and/or mitigate the physical or transition impacts of climate change. Further, the risks we may be exposed to or the opportunities that may be available to us need to be assessed, quantified where possible, and have an appropriate level of control and oversight by management and the Board. Since 2009 we have progressively reduced the emissions from our operations, for example the energy that powers our branches and buildings. This now makes up less than 1% of our total emissions. However, the emissions associated with the lending we provide to our customers is more than 99% of our total emissions. Importantly, much of the emissions produced by our customers and suppliers come from activities or actions that are not within the Bank’s direct control or are more challenging to influence. We acknowledge encouraging behavioural shifts or action on climate change can be challenging, take time and requires trust. How to read our sector-level charts There are five key concepts to understand our sector-level financed emissions progress. 1 Baseline: reflects our portfolio’s starting point in terms of absolute emissions or emissions intensity. 2 Actual: our portfolio’s financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity for a given financial year. 3 Reference scenario: the science-based scenario we currently use to inform our goal or target and what we compare our portfolio’s financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity to. We expect to review these over time. 4 CBA portfolio: an assessment of how the portfolio’s financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity estimate for the current reporting period compares to the reference scenario at the same point in time. 5 Goal or target: our financed absolute emissions or emissions intensity goal or target for the portfolio to be achieved by 2030. For some sectors the charts do not include the baseline or actual to protect our customers’ confidentiality. This is to support cases where, for example, only one customer has drawn lending in the reporting period. For some sectors, our baseline absolute emissions or emissions intensity is not the same as the reference scenario base year. For example, where our portfolio is not representative of the relevant Australian or global sector, to account for the impacts of COVID-19 on the sector, or due to data limitations. This year we have taken the opportunity to clarify how we classify our aspirations as goals or targets. This resulted in some previously reported targets now being described as goals, supporting our continuous efforts to enhance the accuracy and transparency of our reporting. This change is intended to better align to where our pathways for achieving outcomes are subject to key external dependencies, for example the pace of Australia’s energy transition. We have set 10 goals and five targets covering 71% of CBA’s in-scope drawn lending. For several of these sectors, including Australian housing, Australian commercial property and aluminium, lower emissions are heavily reliant on grid decarbonisation. Should the electricity grid not decarbonise at the expected rate, or if State or Federal Government policy settings do not support decarbonisation, then achieving our goals for these sectors will be made more challenging. Sector overview and outlook As at 30 June 2024, lending to the power generation sector represented only 0.5% of our in-scope drawn lending and 1.9% of our financed emissions. In 2023, Scope 1 emissions from the power generation sector accounted for approximately 34% of Australia’s total emissions.1 Retiring coal-fired power stations and shifting to renewable sources of energy is critical to reducing the emissions intensity of Australia’s electricity grid. Renewable electricity can provide a cost-effective way of reducing emissions for consumers and is not only essential for the nation to meet its decarbonisation ambitions, but also to support Australian households and other sectors in reducing their emissions. In the 2024 Integrated System Plan (ISP), AEMO’s step change scenario projects that up to 90% of the National Energy Market’s coal-fired power stations will retire by 2035 with the remaining 10% retiring by 2040. Renewable energy connected with transmission and distribution, firmed with storage and backed up by gas-powered generation, is the lowest-cost way to supply electricity to homes and businesses as Australia transitions to a net zero economy.2 Our target, portfolio and progress Our interim 2030 target is 105 kgCO2/MWh which is a 53% reduction compared to a 2020 baseline. As at 30 June 2024, the emissions intensity of our portfolio was 91 kgCO2/MWh, a reduction of 131 kgCO2/MWh compared to our 2020 baseline and 33 kgCO2/MWh compared to 30 June 2023. Our portfolio was also 73% below the reference scenario. The reduction in our portfolio emissions intensity was primarily driven by lower exposures to non-renewable power generation customers, new drawn lending to the renewables sector and changes in customer emissions. While the emissions intensity of our portfolio has continued to decrease since June 2020, drawdowns of unused lending limits could change our share of customers’ emissions and generation resulting in potential fluctuations in emissions intensity. Our power generation portfolio is diversified by technology and geography with over 50% of our lending exposures outside Australia. Our power generation portfolio is also 72% weighted to lending to solar and wind generation assets, 13% to other renewable generation assets, along with smaller drawn exposures to electricity generators and gentailers that are more emissions-intensive. AEMO’s 2025 Gas Statement of Opportunities forecasts shortfall risks under peak conditions from 2028, three years later than forecast in 2024. Reviewing our operational emissions strategy and targets This year we completed an evaluation of our operational emissions strategy as part of our five-year review cycle. The review considered our Scope 1 and 2, and Scope 3 reduction targets, boundaries and inventories, and incoming new mandatory climate reporting requirements. Given the significant progress in executing our reduction strategies for Scope 1 and 2, we are increasing our reduction target from 42% to 75% by 2030 against our 2020 baseline. We are also able to expand our Scope 1 and 2 target coverage from 2026 onwards as we now have better data for our other overseas offices, including India. We have also made several changes to improve how we measure, manage and represent Scope 3 operational emission sources, particularly those associated with our supply chain. Where we do not currently have activity data available, we are developing spend-based estimates. We have conservatively estimated our expanded footprint as an increase of approximately 600% from our reported 2024 operational emissions. As our current Scope 3 target accounts for only 13% of our expanded estimated emissions, the existing Scope 3 target is no longer meaningful in its present form. Accordingly, we will reassess this target and focus on more accurately quantifying our Scope 3 operational emissions in line with new mandatory climate reporting requirements in 2026. Continuing to support Australian agriculture The Australian agriculture sector is essential for our economy and food security, and is central to regional communities and the financial health of their economies. The sector accounts for 18% of Australia’s net emissions, or 16% excluding land-use, land-use change and forestry. 1 Landowners face risks including acute weather events, a changing climate and loss of ecosystem services. However, many are exploring options to reduce net emissions for improved profitability, enhancements to natural capital for production, and incentives in environmental markets and schemes. Availability and costs to implement new technologies, and balancing competing land uses in the agriculture industry, continue to slow the pace of progress on emissions reductions for the sector. The Bank has been supporting the Australian agriculture sector for over 100 years, and we intend to continue supporting our farmers through our lending and other activities. We recognise that our customers are at different stages of adopting decarbonisation activities and responding to the transition. We partner with companies like Ruminati to provide our farming customers with complimentary tools to estimate their baseline emissions and develop tailored action plans to help them reduce their on-farm emissions. Our approach to climate-related risks and opportunities Climate change has been identified as a risk that could have a material impact on stakeholders within our value chain and expose the Bank to both physical and transition risks. While our current analysis shows that climate change is unlikely to have material financial impacts on the Bank in the short term, failure to respond adequately to the potential and expected impacts of climate change could affect our long-term strategy, performance and franchise value. We acknowledge some of our customers, communities and regions will face greater climate impacts and risks than others, and we remain well positioned to support them. The Bank manages risks, including climate-related risks, through our RMF. The RMF is reviewed by management, the Risk & Compliance Committee and the Board to accommodate changes in our operating environment, better practices, and regulatory and community expectations. Climate-related risks are embedded in the Board-approved risk taxonomy under our E&S risk type. E&S risk is integrated into the Bank’s governance structures, policies, risk appetite and strategic planning processes. E&S risk includes climate- and nature-related impacts, and represents drivers of potentially material strategic, financial and non-financial risks to the Bank. We use a range of tools and techniques to help us identify, assess, manage and monitor climate-related risks holistically at the Group level, and on a portfolio basis or for individual customers in certain circumstances. This approach helps us explore the physical and transition risks from climate change that may impact our business and customers over different time horizons. It also helps us consider how our business activities can impact the environment, our customers and the community. We also perform transition and physical risk scenario analyses to evaluate the resilience of the Bank’s strategy and business model to climate-related changes, developments and uncertainties. Our climate scenario analysis, combined with our climate risk materiality assessment (CRMA), helps us understand our exposure to strategic, financial and non-financial risks from climate change, as well as our risks and opportunities over the short, medium and long term. We continue to enhance our climate risk management tools and practices in line with evolving industry practices, and regulatory expectations. For more information on our approach to managing risks and risk governance, see pages 60–63. ESG Credit Standard We have explicitly incorporated the consideration of ESG risk assessments into our credit risk framework through our ESG Credit Standard. The standard provides a structured framework for the way in which E&S risks are to be considered in credit risk assessment processes for our customers. Along with all our other group-wide credit standards, it establishes the minimum credit expectations and requirements for identifying, managing and monitoring a borrower or counterparty’s E&S risks. The standard, which is applicable across the Bank, requires that existing or new non-retail borrowers or counterparties that meet certain criteria be considered against the commitments in the Bank’s E&S Framework when performing a credit assessment. Throughout the credit process, E&S risks identified are assessed for their impact on our customers’ ability to repay. In some cases, the standard also requires reviewing the borrower’s collateral they pledge to the Bank for E&S risks. We have not currently identified a globally accepted, standardised methodology for quantifying climate-related impacts on credit risk. Therefore, our ESG credit assessments continue to be driven by customer due diligence and qualitative assessments in processes tailored to the risk of specific portfolios. We expect our approach to integrating ESG into our credit risk framework will continue to evolve and adapt as industry practices mature, and as regulatory and stakeholder expectations change. Risk appetite statement The Board-approved RAS defines the maximum risk allowable to deliver the Bank’s strategic priorities. Management is required to operate within risk appetite. We have integrated two quantitative RAS indicators to help minimise potential credit losses from portfolios with higher exposure to climate-related risks. These focus on physical risk in the retail portfolio and transition risk in the institutional portfolio. For home loans, our indicator measures the percentage of loans with high loan-to-value ratios and exposure to climate physical risks like floods, fires and cyclones. This helps monitor the likelihood of higher credit losses if property values fall in areas experiencing extreme weather. For institutional lending, the indicator tracks the percentage of loans to customers with high climate transition risk. This assesses the potential for credit losses if these customers’ businesses are challenged by new climate policies, technology changes or shifting community expectations. Currently, both indicators are within Board-approved thresholds, requiring no intervention. Management reviews these indicators quarterly and adjusts lending policies and limits as needed. The Bank also continues to maintain a qualitative RAS to guide employees on the broader behavioural expectations in relation to our E&S Framework and commitments. The Board reviews and approves the RAS indicators annually. In the latest review, the Board increased the ‘early warning’ and ‘intervention’ levels for the institutional RAS indicator due to a methodology change, not an increased risk appetite. ESG

The scenarios we performed this year Long-term scenarios This year we performed three long-term climate scenarios based on the NGFS scenarios. They explore futures with high transition risk (net zero 2050), higher transition risk (delayed transition) and higher physical risk (current policies). These three NGFS scenarios were selected to enable the assessment of a range of plausible climate physical and transition risk outcomes. To date, global progress against the goals of the Paris Agreement has lagged, increasing risk of the net zero 2050 scenario being out of reach. The delayed transition and current policies scenarios were selected as the Bank believes slower global progress in climate policy increases the probability of either scenario occurring. The NGFS scenario macroeconomic forecasts were tailored to the Australian context by an external economic advisory firm (Oxford Economics), and then modelled using the Bank’s suite of stress testing models to determine balance sheet and credit loss results extending out to 2050. The purpose of these NGFS-aligned scenarios is to identify impact trends that climate change could have over time on the broader economy, certain industry sectors and ultimately the Bank. The scenarios do not attempt to predict the timing and severity of individual acute physical or abrupt transition events that could impact the Bank’s financial performance in any given year. Rather, the cumulative effects of such events are factored into macroeconomic variables used to model these trends. Although this approach enables a clearer view of any trends over time, it likely underestimates potential losses to the Bank because it does not account for localised declines, or direct impacts on, asset values from severe climate physical or transition events that could occur in any given year. Therefore, three acute, event-driven scenarios were conducted to supplement this view (see pages 152–153). Why we ran this scenario Research indicates that large, populated areas across South-East QLD and Northern NSW may experience more severe cyclones in the future as cyclones begin to track further south. We ran this scenario to enhance our understanding of the potential losses to the Bank from an extreme weather event that may become increasingly plausible over time. Key scenario assumptions The scenario assumes two severe cyclones (Category 4) make landfall over South-East QLD a year apart. First over the Sunshine Coast and then Brisbane. Each of these Category 4 cyclones are currently individually assessed as 1-in-200-year events, however the probability of two severe cyclone events in successive years in this location is currently extremely low. This scenario results in significant property damage from wind, storm surges and inland cyclone-induced flooding. This is exacerbated where properties are not built to withstand Category 4 cyclone winds. Limited government support is assumed. Supply chain disruptions and downtime impact business productivity. Following the back-to-back cyclones, property prices decline in impacted areas and the events lead to an economic decline in QLD with unemployment rates increasing materially, particularly in regional areas. Insights from our analysis Total losses to the Bank modelled in this scenario are approximately $1.5 billion over a five-year period, with more than 75% of the losses occurring in the first two years. These losses arise from home loan exposures in impacted areas of approximately $91 billion and non-retail exposures of $16 billion. Losses are approximately double in the retail portfolio compared to non-retail. Mortgage losses are driven by borrower repayment stress after accounting for insurance, coupled with property price declines in impacted areas. Non-retail losses are driven by downtime, supply chain disruptions and economic decline that culminates after the second event. The largest non-retail losses arise from commercial property and wholesale trade. Although not modelled under this scenario, losses could also be expected from personal loans and credit cards, at similar rates to those modelled under the economic downturn stress tests. Although this represents an increase in single year credit losses, it is currently not considered to be financially material to the Bank due to its low probability of occurring and is mitigated by our existing credit provisions. An event of this magnitude would also not impact our current capital or liquidity RAS indicators. Our climate risk materiality assessment approach The CRMA describes the current and anticipated effects of climate-related risks and opportunities on the resilience of the Bank’s strategy, business model and value chain. The CRMA assesses how current and anticipated climate-related risks and opportunities arising from each of the futures outlined in our long-term scenarios, may impact the Bank’s material risk types, strategy, business model and value chain across the current, short, medium and long term. The assessment of impacts to our material non-financial and strategic risk types was performed through workshops with senior management and risk type owners, including ASB. The assessment of financial risk impacts incorporated outcomes from both the long-term and acute scenarios performed this year: • The long-term scenarios provided a perspective on impact trends that climate change could have over time on the broader economy, certain industry sectors and the Bank. • The acute event scenarios enabled us to assess the ability of the Bank to withstand severe, yet plausible, events that could occur in any given year under these futures. The anticipated effects on the Bank under these scenarios were considered across four time horizons: • Current term (within the next 12 months). • Short term (~3 years) to align with the Bank’s strategic planning cycle. • Medium term (~10 years) to align with the timeframe of when physical impacts begin to diverge for the low versus high warming futures. • Long term (~30 years) to align with the Bank’s home loan portfolio where home loans can be contractually agreed to for up to 30 years. The risk ratings indicate the impact of climate change on the relevant risk type under each scenario. For financial risks and capital adequacy risk, ratings were determined with reference to the relevant Board approved RAS. For non-financial, E&S and AI risks our 5x5 risk matrix was applied. Risk appetite statement – Risk ratings were set based on the expected position relative to the relevant Board approved RAS thresholds. For example, a financial impact resulting in the Bank being outside risk appetite would be rated as ‘very high risk’. 5x5 risk matrix – Our risk matrix, updated in 2025, considers the impact and expected frequency of a risk eventuating, resulting in risks being rated as either low, moderate, medium, high or very high risk. Impact and frequency are assessed using the following: • Expected frequency ranges from ‘1 event every 10 years’ to ‘Multiple events in the next year’; and • Impacts uses a combination of qualitative factors and financial measures. Qualitative factors consider impacts on customers, our operations and people, shareholders, communities, and regulatory and legal. The quantitative financial impacts range from negligible ≤$1 million; minor >$1 million; major >$5

risks being rated as either low, moderate, medium, high or very high risk. Impact and frequency are assessed using the following: • Expected frequency ranges from ‘1 event every 10 years’ to ‘Multiple events in the next year’; and • Impacts uses a combination of qualitative factors and financial measures. Qualitative factors consider impacts on customers, our operations and people, shareholders, communities, and regulatory and legal. The quantitative financial impacts range from negligible ≤$1 million; minor >$1 million; major >$5 million; significant >$25 million; or critical >$100 million. For example, a medium risk rating could arise from an event expected to occur once every 10 years, with a significant financial impact of $25 million to $100 million. Alternatively, a medium risk rating could also arise from multiple events expected to occur in the next year, but with a minor impact of $1 million to $5 million. Each risk was assessed based on its impact to the Bank in the time horizon in which the relevant scenario occurs, rather than cumulative impacts over all time horizons. When assessing impacts for future time horizons under these scenarios, no additional material changes to the business model or control environment were assumed beyond those already in place. For example, while a potential strategic shift could mitigate some risks in the future, such changes were not factored into the future risk ratings. We acknowledge that available data and techniques to perform this type of assessment are still maturing across the industry. As a result, our assessment of the impacts of climate-related risks involves a greater reliance on assumptions than is typically required for more mature risk types, where historical data is a better predictor of future events. As data and assessment techniques improve over time, we anticipate that our future CRMAs will incorporate more advanced assessment techniques. Current and anticipated impacts on our financial statements Current year impact on our financial statements The Bank monitors its financial performance, financial position and cashflow on an ongoing basis through its governance structure. Climate-related effects can be widespread and interrelated, and may influence our operations, strategy and financial outcomes over the short, medium and long term. As per the result of our CRMA, no climate-related risks or opportunities were noted this year that have had a material impact on the Bank’s financial performance, financial position or cash flows. Anticipated impacts on our financial statements In some years, the Bank may experience increases in credit losses due to extreme weather events, however the scenario results indicate that financial impacts to the Bank from climate-related impacts are not expected to be material. This reflects the nature of our operations, the sectors in which we operate, and our existing risk management frameworks and portfolio diversification, which together provide a degree of resilience against potential climate-related impacts. The Bank is well placed to identify and pursue available opportunities arising from Australia’s transition to net zero by 2050. For example, the development of sustainable finance products, tools and services to support customers to transition and adapt to the impacts of climate change. While climate change presents challenges to the Australian economy and our communities, our core business remains resilient. A relatively small proportion of the Group’s TCE is currently exposed to high or very high physical or transition risk. Our customers have historically demonstrated strong repayment performance and we have established support mechanisms to assist them in times of financial stress, including those potentially arising from climate-related events. Although severe climate-related events could result in an increase in single year credit losses, these losses are assessed as a medium risk to the Bank as they would not result in a breach of our current capital, liquidity or profitability RAS indicators. This reflects our strong provisioning levels and capital position. The CSI tool forecasts climate stress through to 2030 by postcode, based on key agri-climatic productivity variables across grain, livestock and dairy sectors. The tool enables our bankers to have conversations with customers on their long-term climate adaptation plans relevant for credit risk assessment. CSI insights are also used for portfolio monitoring in livestock, grain and dairy commodities, helping us track exposure trends and inform strategic planning. Insights from the tool can be shared with customers through a Climate Insight Report, tailored to their region and commodities, to help them consider the data and plan for future climate-related resilience. We will retire our productivity mapping tool given the launch of the CSI which provides a forward view of climate risk. Reconciliation of Group total committed exposures to lending used for financed emissions calculations In-scope drawn lending refers to the on-balance sheet exposure to the sectors included within the scope of our financed emissions calculations. Some asset classes and sectors we lend to are currently excluded due to lack of available data, methodologies and/or relevance. The in- scope TCE lending portfolio excludes exposures to finance and insurance, government administration and defence ANZSICs, and non-lending products. The in-scope TCE lending portfolio assessed excludes exposures that are not assessed, which includes consumer finance (excluding Australian motor vehicle finance) and commercial property outside of Australia and New Zealand. Our financed emissions estimates are based on our drawn lending only, in line with the PCAF Standard’s use of outstanding amounts. Undrawn loan commitments are not included. As at 30 June 2024, we have estimated financed emissions over our in-scope assessed portfolio, covering drawn lending of $860.5 billion. The in-scope drawn lending portfolio assessed represents 62% of total TCE. Financed emissions continued Financed emissions portfolio analysis Our calculations cover 96% of our in-scope drawn lending exposure. Movements in the overall absolute financed emissions and emissions intensity of our in-scope drawn lending portfolio are generally dependent on changes in our portfolio mix over time and differences in emissions profiles at the sector or customer level. We estimate our 2024 absolute financed emissions for our in-scope lending portfolio at 22.6 MtCO2-e, an increase of 9% (+1.8 MtCO2-e), compared to the restated 2023 absolute financed emissions estimate (20.8 MtCO2-e). Most notable increases were observed in the transport and storage, and manufacturing sectors. These movements were partly offset by reductions in estimated absolute emissions in the mining sector. Sustainability Funding Target Tracking towards our Sustainability Funding Target As at 30 June 2025, we have provided $64.4 billion in cumulative funding towards our Sustainability Funding Target (SFT) of $70 billion by 2030. Given the recent release of the Australian Sustainable Finance Taxonomy and in light of reaching more than 92% of our 2030 target this year, we will review our target and eligibility criteria next year. ASB separately tracks and measures the funding they provide towards their SFT. Since 2022 ASB has provided a cumulative NZ $2.1 billion in funding towards their target of NZ $6.5 billion by 2030. For more information on our SFT criteria, see pages 416–418 in the Climate disclosures appendix. Our SFT monitors the level of cumulative funding within the scope of our SFT eligibility criteria. Investment: Climate-related investment refers to capital deployed through financial instruments or equity stakes in public or private markets that relate to the Bank’s climate-related risks or opportunities and where climate considerations form a material part of the investment rationale or potential outcomes. This year CBA invested $46 million in climate-related investments. Expenditure: Climate-related expenditure refers to capital or operational spending incurred in managing climate-related risks or pursuing climate-related opportunities. This includes direct costs related to internal systems, infrastructure, tools or processes that are focused on climate risk mitigation, adaptation or resilience. No material direct climate-related expenditure was noted this year. Indirect costs include ongoing expenditure which would be incurred ordinarily, making it impractical to allocate costs as specifically climate-related. Overseeing executive performance and remuneration outcomes One of the Board’s responsibilities is to establish and assess executive performance and remuneration targets and outcomes. Remuneration decisions In determining executive remuneration, the Board considered financial and non-financial performance outcomes in the context of the 2025 financial year and over a multi-year period. To better align our pay against the ASX (including peer banks) and offshore comparator groups, fixed remuneration (FR) increases ranged from 4.5% to 16.7%. The CEO’s FR was adjusted by 14% which is the first increase received since the 2022 financial year. This increase reflects the CEO’s demonstrated strong performance, capability, and the size and scale of the Bank relative to peers. The FY25 realised remuneration for the CEO was $7.02m, a decrease of 22% from FY24. FY25 realised remuneration for the CEO and Group Executives (GE) reflects the longer deferral periods of the executive remuneration framework implemented in the 2021 financial year and includes 2022 and 2023 deferred short-term variable remuneration (STVR), and FY21 long-term alignment remuneration (LTAR). The Board also approved: • FY25 STVR outcomes ranging between 74% and 88% of maximum. • FY25 LTAR awarded with no reduction following the pre-grant assessment. • Vesting of the FY22 LTAR award with no reduction (50% for the CEO and 100% for GEs), following Board review of multi-year leadership and strategic execution, and risk outcomes for individual executives. Audit Committee Assesses and advises the People & Remuneration Committee of any audit matters which may impact collective and/or individual remuneration outcomes. Nominations Committee Considers and reviews matters relevant to evaluating the performance of the CEO and reports the evaluation to the People & Remuneration Committee and the Board. Risk & Compliance Committee Advises the People & Remuneration Committee of material risk matters which may impact collective and/or individual remuneration outcomes. People & Remuneration Committee and Board oversight The People & Remuneration Committee is the governing body for developing, monitoring and assessing the remuneration strategy and framework across CBA on behalf of the Board, ensuring that these are aligned to regulatory requirements, appropriate and operating as intended. The role of the People & Remuneration Committee is to review, challenge, assess and, as appropriate, endorse the recommendations made by management for Board approval. The Board reviews, challenges, applies judgement and, as appropriate, approves the People & Remuneration Committee’s recommendations. The People & Remuneration Committee met formally eight times during the 2025 financial year with the following members (as at 30 June 2025): Simon Moutter (Chair), Lyn Cobley, Paul O’Malley and Mary Padbury. The responsibilities of the People & Remuneration Committee are outlined in its Charter, which is reviewed annually. The Charter is available at commbank.com.au/peopleandremuneration As part of the performance and risk review, and to support the determination of remuneration outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives, the People & Remuneration Committee meets concurrently with the Risk & Compliance, Audit, and Nominations Committees. These concurrent meetings provide an opportunity for the Committees to review and recommend relevant risk and audit matters that may warrant consideration in the People & Remuneration Committee’s determination of remuneration outcomes. Information provided to the concurrent meetings supports the review and recommendation of collective and/or individual remuneration arrangements, including outcomes and variable remuneration adjustments. Considerations at the meeting include risk scorecard outcomes for the CEO and Group Executives, details of material risk matters presented by the Group CRO and outcomes of internal audit reviews conducted during the year, presented by the Group Auditor.
